meta.subtitle: Strong June-quarter earnings, but a Bear case back at FY25 earnings holds the call at HOLD

analystCommentary:
Bank of America's June quarter was strong on the bank's own measures: revenue, net of interest expense, rose {+ 15% +} year over year and diluted EPS rose {+ 34% +}. The question for the shares is not the quarter but how much of it repeats.

Two notes on the pack. The vendor's statement templates are built for industrial companies, so the financials section says once which rows do not apply to a bank, and the report works from the 10-Q and the earnings release instead. The headline capture returned the bank's research notes on other companies rather than news about the bank, so the report carries no post-quarter news.

We rate the shares HOLD with a target range of $58–$68. The valuation section sets out why: the call is close to BUY and turns on both the Base multiple and the weight on the Bear case.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Bank of America Corporation is a Delaware bank holding company and financial holding company headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, and it operates its banking activities primarily under the Bank of America, N.A. charter. At June 30, 2026 it had $3.5 trillion in assets and approximately 211,000 employees, with operations across the U.S., its territories and more than 35 countries and/or jurisdictions. It serves more than 69 million consumer and small business clients through approximately 3,500 retail financial centers, approximately 15,000 ATMs and digital banking platforms with approximately 50 million active users.

The 10-Q reports four business segments, Consumer Banking, Global Wealth & Investment Management (GWIM), Global Banking and Global Markets, with the remaining operations in All Other. The vendor's FY25 mix, which the segment chart follows, puts Consumer Banking at 37.4% ($43.7B), Global Wealth and Investment Management at 21.3% ($24.9B), Global Banking at 20.6% ($24.1B) and Global Markets at 20.6% ($24.1B). The vendor's geographic split lists a Non-US total of 12.0% beside the regional figures that make it up, so the chart counts non-U.S. revenue twice; the usable figure is the United States at 76.0%.

Revenue in the June quarter split almost evenly between net interest income and noninterest income, so the bank's earnings rest about equally on the rate and funding cycle and on fees, many of them tied to markets activity.

thesis.body:
The June quarter improved all three of the bank's earnings lines. Net interest income rose {+ 9% +} to $16.0 billion, which the release attributes to Global Markets activity, higher loan and deposit balances and fixed-rate asset repricing, partially offset by the impact of lower interest rates. Noninterest income rose {+ 22% +}, and with noninterest expense up a slower 8% the quarter produced 6.6% of operating leverage; provision for credit losses fell from a year earlier.

The quarter supports the consensus earnings path. What it does not settle is how much of the fee growth repeats, or how far a rate cycle could take net interest income the other way, and a Bear case built on those two risks is why we rate the shares HOLD.

catalysts: Operating leverage running ahead of the expectation management set in April, which it raised mid-year.
A higher quarterly dividend declared in July, alongside continued repurchases.
Loan growth led by commercial lending, with the CEO saying that near-term, pipelines remain strong, and commercial borrowing has picked up.

AI-enabled tools that management says are now more embedded in workflows across operations, risk, finance, technology and client-facing teams; it describes benefits on both the revenue side and the expense side, and the pack quantifies neither.
risks: Rate cuts and their effect on net interest income, the larger of the two revenue lines.
Investment banking and trading revenue at a cyclical high.
Credit losses rising from today's stable run-rate if the economy turns.
Open litigation and regulatory matters, and changes to capital requirements.
A Say on Pay vote that fell short of three-quarters support in 2025.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The vendor's income table is gross of interest expense, so it is not a bank's revenue line. Its revenue series runs from $93.9B in FY21 to $191.6B in FY25, and its gross margin (99.8% in FY21, 56.1% in FY25) is not a franchise measure for a bank. The snapshot's Q2'26 revenue of $49.4B (+6%) is on the same gross basis; the 10-Q and the release report revenue, net of interest expense, of $31.6 billion against $27.4 billion a year earlier, and the report uses that net basis throughout. Consensus FY26E revenue of ~$124B carries no basis note. Our reading is that it sits on the net basis, because the six months to June produced $61,830 million of revenue net of interest expense, about half of that estimate; if so, the -35% shown against FY25 is a change of basis rather than a forecast, and FY27E revenue of $130.5B sits on the same basis. The vendor's operating income ran from $34.0B in FY21 to a low of $28.3B in FY23 and $37.7B in FY25, and FY25 net income was $30.5B.

On the bank's basis, net interest yield on a fully taxable-equivalent basis rose 14 bps year over year to 2.08 percent. The release attributes the rise in noninterest expense equally to revenue-related expenses and investments in people, brand and technology. Pretax income rose to $11.6 billion from $8.7 billion, net income was $9.1 billion against $7.2 billion, and diluted EPS was $1.21 against $0.90; six-month diluted EPS was $2.31 against $1.79. The efficiency ratio improved 359 bps to 59%, return on average assets was 1.03%, return on average common shareholders' equity was 12.7% and return on average tangible common shareholders' equity was 17.0%, up from 13.6% a year earlier.
financials.balanceCommentary:
The vendor's balance-sheet and leverage rows do not apply to a bank either. FY25 total debt of $365.9B and net debt of $134.1B leave out the deposits that fund most of the balance sheet, and the current ratio, trailing net debt to EBITDA of 15.4x and interest coverage of 0.6x treat deposit funding and interest expense as an industrial company's would, so we draw no conclusion from them. The 10-Q gives the usable frame. Total assets were $3,499,191 million at June 30, 2026, up $87.5 billion from December 31, 2025, primarily on securities borrowed or purchased under agreements to resell and customer receivables supporting Global Markets client activity and on commercial loan growth, partially offset by lower debt securities. Total deposits of $2,025,124 million exceeded total loans and leases of $1,217,619 million, and the release puts average Global Liquidity Sources at $947 billion.

Capital is the binding constraint. CET1 capital was $202 billion, up $1.9 billion from the March quarter, and the CET1 ratio was 11.2% on the standardized approach, which management says is well ahead of its 10% minimum; risk-weighted assets rose to $1.8 trillion on loan growth and capital markets activity. Total shareholders' equity fell $2.1 billion from December 31, 2025 to $301,094 million, which the 10-Q attributes primarily to repurchases, dividends, lower accumulated other comprehensive income and a preferred stock redemption, partially offset by net income. Book value and tangible book value per common share each rose 7% over the year.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash flow is the least informative statement for a bank. The vendor's operating cash flow moves from $45.0B in FY23 to -$8.8B in FY24 and $12.6B in FY25, the table shows capital expenditure of $0.00, and free cash flow therefore repeats operating cash flow. The trailing FCF yield of 22.4% inherits the same problem, and we do not use it.

The capital-return rows do carry information. Share repurchases were $4.6B in FY23, $13.1B in FY24 and $24.1B in FY25, and dividends paid rose each year from $8.1B in FY21 to $9.6B in FY25. Repurchases are the variable part of the payout and dividends the steady part.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
At $59.47 the shares trade at 13.5x trailing earnings, 12.8x NTM earnings and ~11.3x FY27E EPS, with a dividend yield of 1.95%. EV/EBITDA of 24.7x and P/S of 2.2x rest on the vendor's gross revenue and EBITDA and do not apply to a bank, and peer multiples are pending a peer data source, so the page cannot say whether the multiple is cheap or dear against peers. The bank's own anchors are book value per common share of $39.34 and tangible book value per common share of $29.37, on which it earned a return on average tangible common shareholders' equity of 16.52% for the six months.

The Street is constructive: 54 analysts, Buy 35, Hold 18, Sell 1, with a consensus target of $66.00 (+11.0%), a median of $65.00 and a range of $59.00–$75.00. The shares sit in the upper part of their 52-week range of $46.12–$65.23.

Each scenario applies a multiple to the EPS it expects for the year ahead, so the like-for-like reference is today's NTM multiple, not the lower multiple the price implies on FY27E. The Base holds the NTM multiple a year out. For holding it: return on tangible equity has risen over the year, first-half operating leverage ran above the full-year range management now expects, and consensus still has EPS growing into FY27E. Against it: FY27E builds on fee lines at a cyclical high, and a market that comes to see 2026 as a peak in fees would pay less for the next year's earnings. We think the two arguments balance; the Base multiple is one of the two inputs the label turns on, with the Bear weight.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Consensus FY27E EPS is met and 2027 shows it is durable: operating leverage at the top of management's 2026 range and positive again in 2027, credit costs near the current run-rate. The Bull assumes no EPS above consensus, only a higher multiple: 14x, our assumption of a step above the trailing multiple for earnings that have shown they repeat. That is $73.64, just below the top of the Street's target range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus is met: EPS of $4.64 in FY26E and $5.26 in FY27E. In our reading that needs 2027 to add positive operating leverage and continued loan growth on top of a strong 2026, with fees holding up and repricing keeping net interest income growing as rates fall. The CET1 ratio stays near its June level with repurchases absorbing the excess, and the shares hold today's 12.8x NTM multiple a year out, applied to FY27E EPS. That is $67.33, close to the Street's consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Rate cuts compress net interest income faster than repricing offsets them, trading and investment banking fall back toward year-ago levels, and provision rises as credit normalizes, so EPS returns to the FY25 level of $3.82. A market pricing falling earnings pays less than the Base's NTM multiple; we assume 12x, a small discount because capital and deposits stay intact. That is $45.84, just under the 52-week low.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base at 55%, the Bull at 25% and the Bear at 20%. The weighted fair value is $64.61, an expected upside of +8.6%, against a bear-case downside of -22.9% and a reward/risk of 0.38×. That derives HOLD. The Base sits above the price, so the label does not say the shares are expensive; it is HOLD because the Bear downside is large beside the expected upside, which leaves reward/risk short of the 0.50× a BUY needs, and expected upside is also short of the +10.0% threshold.

Each weight rests on evidence about the year the scenarios price. The Base gets most of the weight because the evidence for 2027 points to consensus as the central path: loans grew in every business segment, commercial borrowing has picked up, and in our reading consensus needs positive operating leverage in 2027, not a repeat of 2026's pace. Against it stands the rate mechanism, which works on 2027 net interest income whatever 2026 delivered. The Bull gets a quarter because 2026 is running above management's own expectation, but it needs the fee lines to hold at a cyclical high for another year. The Bear gets less than the Bull because it needs the downturn the risk section describes, and the current credit evidence runs the other way; it is not smaller, because the rate mechanism and the fee cycle are both live.

The call is close to BUY. Holding the Bear at today's NTM multiple instead of our discounted one lifts expected upside to just under the BUY threshold; a Base at the trailing multiple on FY27E derives a narrow BUY; and moving a third of the Bear weight to the Bull case does the same. Moving a quarter of it lifts expected upside past the threshold but leaves reward/risk under its bar, which is the test that binds. In the other direction, a Base at 12x FY27E, our assumption for a modest de-rating, or swapping the Bull and Bear weights, still derives HOLD, as does a heavier Bear on top of that lower Base. We think the NTM multiple on FY27E is the honest Base and that the Bear multiple belongs below it.

segments.name: Consumer Banking Segment
segments.body: Consumer Banking is the deposit engine. June-quarter revenue was $11,336 million, up 5%, driven primarily by higher net interest income, and net income was $3,281 million; provision fell to $1.2 billion with a net reserve release of $23 million against a net reserve build of $82 million a year earlier. The efficiency ratio was 51% and the return on average allocated capital 29%. Average deposits of $957 billion are up from pre-pandemic levels per the release, 59% of deposits sit in checking accounts, and the release ranks the bank first in U.S. consumer deposits on first-quarter 2026 FFIEC call-report data. The card book's risk-adjusted margin, what it earns after losses, fell to 6.5% from 7.1% a year earlier while average balances grew to $103.6 billion; the pack gives no cause for the decline.

segments.name: Global Wealth and Investment Management Segment
segments.body: GWIM revenue rose 16% to $6,871 million on asset management fees up 19% to $4.4 billion, which the release attributes to higher market valuations and solid AUM flows, as well as higher NII; net income rose to $1,413 million from $993 million, and the pretax margin reached 27% from 22% a year earlier. Client balances were $4.9 trillion, up 12% driven primarily by higher market valuations, and assets under management $2.3 trillion, up 17%, with AUM flows of $13.7 billion in the quarter and $78 billion since the second quarter of 2025. Average loans and leases rose 14% to $270 billion. Fee revenue here moves with markets, and a quarter's flows are small beside the balances they are added to.

segments.name: Global Banking Segment
segments.body: Global Banking is the corporate lending, treasury and investment banking franchise. Per the call, revenue rose 10% to $6.2 billion and net income 20% to more than $2 billion, with total corporate investment banking fees, excluding self-led deals, up 50% to more than $2.1 billion across debt underwriting, advisory and equity underwriting. Average deposits rose 8% to $652 billion and average loans 7% to $413 billion, the release cites higher treasury service charges, and the return on allocated capital was 15%. The pack shows the fee growth but not whether it reflects share gains or a strong market, so we read it as mostly market conditions.

segments.name: Global Markets Segment
segments.body: Global Markets produced the quarter's sharpest growth. Sales and trading revenue was $7.1 billion including net DVA losses of $57 million, up 33% including and excluding net DVA, with equities up 70% to $3.6 billion on client financing activity and trading in derivatives and cash, and FICC up 9% to $3.5 billion; segment net income was $2.6 billion, and $2.7 billion excluding DVA per the call. The release counts 17 consecutive quarters of year-over-year sales and trading growth, and the call adds 14 consecutive quarters of year-over-year net income growth, which shows a franchise that has grown through several market conditions; whether it gained share the pack cannot say. It is also the segment most directly exposed to a market downturn.

moatFactors.name: Deposit franchise
moatFactors.body: Average deposits of $2.02 trillion grew for a 12th consecutive quarter of sequential average growth per the release, and the call puts the rate paid on consumer deposits at 48 basis points. Low-cost, growing deposits fund the loan book with room to spare and are the base of net interest income. The pressure point is the net interest yield: if deposit costs rise faster than asset yields reprice, that yield is where it shows.

moatFactors.name: Scale and digital distribution
moatFactors.body: The branch, ATM and digital footprint in the company overview is the distribution base, and the release reports that most Consumer Banking sales were digitally enabled, with 4.4 billion digital logins and 24.6 million active Erica users in the quarter. In our view that scale is what lets the bank keep investing in technology, brand and people while improving its efficiency ratio. Scale also concentrates operational and regulatory exposure.

moatFactors.name: Integrated model
moatFactors.body: The call describes the connectivity between markets, Global Banking and Wealth and Investment Management as creating value for clients. Within Consumer Banking the release reports 38.7 million consumer checking accounts, 92% of them primary, and $640 billion of consumer investment assets, up 18% with $19 billion of net client flows, and ~6K net new $500K+ relationships were added across Merrill and the Private Bank in the quarter. Integration cuts both ways: the wealth and markets businesses are the ones most sensitive to asset prices, so the model raises the sensitivity of earnings to markets as well as the stickiness of clients.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat wide because its base, the deposit franchise, is in place and growing, and because scale and the connections between the businesses reinforce it. Three things could erode it: a rate path that lifts deposit costs while asset yields fall, credit losses above the current run-rate, and a reset of capital rules that limits how much the bank can grow and return. Whether the franchise lasts is a separate question from whether the June quarter's fee revenue repeats, and we keep the two apart.

points: Management now expects full-year 2026 operating leverage of 300-400 basis points, after first-half operating leverage exceeded 450 basis points, up from the more than 200 basis points it guided in April. The sustainable aim it described at Investor Day sits below that range, so 2026 is running above the aim and 2027 starts from a high base.

Net interest income for the six months was $31,742 million against $29,113 million a year earlier, and the call adds the repayment of higher-cost funding to the repricing the release cites. Continued growth depends on repricing outrunning lower rates.

Average loans and leases of $1.22 trillion rose 8% from a year ago, with growth in every business segment and a ninth consecutive quarter of sequential average growth; average commercial loans rose 11% to $733 billion. Growth led by commercial lending also concentrates the credit exposure the risk section watches.

Fee lines are growing faster than the balance sheet: the call cites 18% growth in investment brokerage fees, and wealth fees rose with market valuations as well as flows, so part of that growth is the market rather than the franchise.

Client growth underneath: 160K+ net new consumer checking accounts and 30 consecutive quarters of net growth, and ~2 million BofA Rewards enrollments in the quarter after the late-May relaunch; these feed next year's deposits and fees.

management.leadership: Brian T. Moynihan is Chair and CEO, as the July 14, 2026 release styles him, and the March 2026 proxy names Mr. Nowell as Lead Independent Director. The proxy reports that the Board determined every director and nominee other than Mr. Moynihan to be independent under the NYSE listing standards and its Categorical Standards. Alastair M. Borthwick is Executive Vice President and CFO per the release. On execution the record is the quarter: per the call, every business segment grew revenue and net income, generated operating leverage and improved its efficiency ratio, and the full-year operating-leverage expectation was raised mid-year rather than defended. In our view that is good evidence of cost discipline alongside continued investment.
management.capitalAllocation: The bank returned $8.0 billion in the June quarter, $2.0 billion in common dividends and $6.0 billion in repurchases, close to the quarter's net income, so repurchases carry most of the payout and the dividend yield understates it. On July 23, 2026 the Board declared a quarterly dividend of $0.32, payable September 25, 2026, an increase of 14 percent over the prior quarterly dividend of $0.28. The limit is regulatory capital: returning most of earnings holds the CET1 ratio steady only while risk-weighted assets grow moderately, and the 10-Q lists the impact of adverse changes to total loss-absorbing capacity requirements, stress capital buffer requirements and global systemically important bank surcharges among its uncertainties. Our judgment is that the allocation is disciplined and the dividend increase affordable; the risk is a rule change that lowers the ceiling, not a management choice.
management.governance: The March 2026 proxy is the source. Say on Pay drew 73.6% of approximately 5.6 billion votes cast at the 2025 annual meeting. The proxy says shareholder engagement and its assessment of the vote informed the decision to keep the executive compensation design generally consistent; it attributes the higher performance standard for a 100% payout on the performance restricted stock units granted in February 2026, and the new opportunity to earn up to 150% maximum payout, to the focus on long-term Responsible Growth discussed with investors at the 2025 Investor Day. In our reading a vote below three-quarters is the weakest signal in the proxy, mitigated by an otherwise independent board and a Lead Independent Director. The related-person policy covers transactions expected to exceed $120,000 in which the company is a participant and a related person has a direct or indirect material interest, requires the Corporate Governance Committee to approve or ratify them, and exempts types the Board has determined involve no such interest. The excerpt does not carry the pay tables, so we make no claim about pay levels.
management.insiderOwnership: The March 2026 proxy's ownership table is as of March 13, 2026, except where its footnotes say otherwise. Each director and named executive officer, and all directors and executive officers as a group of 25 persons, beneficially owned less than 1% of the common stock. Mr. Moynihan beneficially owned 2,803,195 shares, with a further 1,724,434 stock units, for 4,527,629 in total, and the group held 18,963,591 shares and units combined. As reported in the proxy, three holders were above 5%: The Vanguard Group at 9.1%, Warren E. Buffett/Berkshire Hathaway Inc. at 7.9% (568,070,012 shares) and BlackRock, Inc. at 6.9%. For outside holders, the Berkshire Hathaway position is the one tied to a single named filer rather than an asset manager; in our reading a holder of that size can be heard on capital return and succession in a way a diversified manager usually is not, and the capital-return policy this report credits operates with that holder on the register. The pack carries no statement of its intentions or votes. Insider holdings are meaningful to the executives personally but immaterial to control, and the pack carries no insider transaction data.

idiosyncratic: Rate cycle and net interest income. The February 2026 10-K says a change in monetary policy resulting in lower interest rates would typically result in lower revenue through lower net interest income, and notes that the Federal Reserve reduced policy rates in 2025 with uncertainty over the pace and duration of further reductions. The June-quarter release already shows the effect, with NII growth partially offset by the impact of lower interest rates. Net interest income is the larger of the two revenue lines, so the pace of cuts against the pace of repricing is the Bear case's first mechanism.

Fees at the top of the cycle. Per the call, revenue growth was led by NII, investment banking, wealth management fees and sales and trading, and the CEO, in the release, called it an exceptional quarter for the markets-facing businesses. The 10-K says a market downturn could reduce noninterest income as well as net interest income. A return to year-ago levels in investment banking and trading would remove much of the quarter's revenue growth, and the equities line, whose growth outpaced FICC's, is the one we would watch first.

Credit normalization. Provision and net charge-offs of $1.4 billion each were relatively flat to the March quarter and below a year earlier. Per the call, consumer card charge-offs and delinquencies improved year over year and quarter over quarter, and reservable criticized commercial exposures fell approximately $2.3 billion from the March quarter to roughly $22 billion. The signal to watch is the call's other side: CRE improvement was offset by some isolated corporate and commercial lending losses. The 10-Q names the risk, future credit losses higher than currently expected.

Litigation, regulation and operational exposure. The 10-Q's forward-looking statement lists open matters, including unemployment-benefit processing for California and certain other states, the automatic credit card payment service, anti-money-laundering and economic sanctions programs, and Zelle-related fraud, along with potential changes to loss allocations between financial institutions and customers. None is quantified in the pack, and the bank's own statement that future liabilities may be in excess of its recorded liability and estimated range of possible loss is the risk in its own words.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposures are those of a global systemically important bank. The February 2026 10-K's market risk factor runs from interest rates, inflation and Federal Reserve policy through fiscal and debt-ceiling risk, tariffs, geopolitical events, bank and nonbank failures and the volatility of digital assets; the 10-Q's forward-looking statement adds sovereign debt stress outside the U.S. and a deterioration in private credit markets. The backdrop on the July 14, 2026 call was benign: the bank's research team had raised its 2026 U.S. GDP growth forecast to 2.2% and expected global growth of 3.2% in 2026 and 3.5% in 2027, and consumer spending was running at 6% plus year over year. A downturn would hit all three earnings lines at once, net interest income through rates, fees through markets and provision through credit, and that is the Bear case's mechanism.

body: **HOLD, target range $58–$68.** Our weighted value of $64.61, an expected upside of +8.6%, falls short of BUY in a close call that turns on both the Base multiple and the Bear weight, as the valuation section shows.
What we value is the deposit and lending franchise and the capital it generates; what holds the label back is the fee and rate exposure the Bear case prices.

On unchanged scenarios, a fall in the price to the bottom of our range would derive BUY, and a rise to just above the top of it would derive SELL. On the evidence, a second half that confirms the raised operating-leverage expectation with credit costs near the current run-rate would support the trailing multiple on FY27E in the Base, which derives BUY; a year-over-year decline in sales and trading or in net interest income would raise the Bear weight.
